I've got a friend who wants to build a PC to create music with a program called aerodrum. He was considering a laptop but I told him that was a bad idea. The minimum CPU requirement for aerodrum is an Intel core 2 duo at 2ghz. I planned a build for him with a core 2 duo 3ghz. The entire build minus the computer screen would only be about 150 euros. A total steal and probably performs better than a 500 Euro laptop. My friend has no interest in gaming. I told him my build was more than adequate for his needs. Is there any negative in the build I suggested?
Any point in not just basing a build around an old CPU?

If you are recording live music to the hard drive, more ram and a fast hard drive with a large cache will help. If possible get a sata6 SSD. That chip should be fine, if you experience recording problems it will be because it ran out of ram or the hard drive was too slow to keep up.

A total steal and probably performs better than a 500 Euro laptop

This part I'd say you're probably wrong on. Substantial advancements in cpu architecture mean that the laptop would almost definitely trounce the core 2 duo in basically every workload. Hell Intel has 4.5w tablet chips that I believe beats the 65w core 2 duos in many workloads now.

Just because the program has a minimum req of core 2 duo doesn't mean it won't be MUCH better on a faster chip. My suggestion is to atleast go in the middle ground and spend ~300 euros to move up the processor and maybe get a tiny SSD

In what way are they better though? Modern chips often have the same or worse speed rating and the bus speed for memory is the same as a 3ghz core 2 duo. There are extra cores and build in graphics with expensive modern chips but I don't think they would be utilised unless you're doing heavy multitasking.

Their instructions per clock are higher, they typically have higher base speeds or atleast much higher burst speeds, their handling of memory/cache is better, plus thousands of other small tweaks in the cores.

Just an example, the 4.5w 5y10(Not even the newest generation of core m, and not even the top-binned chip) gets 2070 in geekbench and the core 2 duo e6700 gets 1500. This is just the first number I found on google, but there was a comparison article I read when the first core m's came out comparing it on a ton of fronts.

My point is simply that we've seen more progress on cpu's than we tend to think.

But what about real world performance? If someone is using a single app that hasn't been optimised for multiple cores how much difference would there be between a duo core 2 @ 3ghz that costs $20 vs a $300 3ghz modern 4 core chip? Most laptops around the $500 range have like a 1.7-2.2ghz 4 core CPU with inbuilt Intel graphics and performance wise they feel really slow and weak.

Real world performance would be much better, I am in the US but jumped on amazon UK and quickly found this-

That was at the top of my results when going for ~500 pounds. There might be better options, but that would be considerably faster than a core 2 duo in day to day usage and in that program.

However I wasn't suggesting a laptop, if you are already willing to do a desktop I'd suggest looking for something from sandy-bridge generation or later and just pocket the difference.
